source: WHO Developmental Milestones & Motor Development Study

milestones.title: Lifts head during tummy time
milestones.description: Head lifting during tummy time is the foundational gross motor milestone for this age group. It indicates developing neck extensor strength and is a prerequisite for all subsequent postural control milestones.
milestones.instruction: Place the baby face-down on a firm, flat surface. Ensure the baby is awake and alert. Wait up to 30 seconds.
milestones.question: Does the baby lift their head, even briefly, while lying on their tummy?

milestones.title: Holds head steady when held upright
milestones.description: Head steadying in an upright position reflects early postural tone development. Persistent head lag at this age is a red flag for hypotonia.
milestones.instruction: Hold the baby in an upright position against your chest with minimal support to the head.
milestones.question: Does the baby hold their head steady without it flopping forward or sideways?

milestones.title: Pushes up on forearms during tummy time
milestones.description: Weight-bearing on forearms during prone position demonstrates progressive upper limb and shoulder girdle development beyond simple head lifting.
milestones.instruction: Place the baby on their tummy on a firm surface. Observe for forearm weight-bearing with chest lift.
milestones.question: Does the baby push up onto their forearms and lift their chest slightly off the surface?

milestones.title: Opens and closes hands
milestones.description: Voluntary hand opening and closing marks the transition from the neonatal grasp reflex to emerging voluntary hand control.
milestones.instruction: Observe the baby's hands during a wakeful, calm period without stimulation.
milestones.question: Does the baby open and close their hands voluntarily during wakeful periods?

milestones.title: Swipes at dangling objects
milestones.description: Swiping at a visually tracked object requires integration of visual tracking and emerging voluntary arm movement — the earliest hand-eye coordination.
milestones.instruction: Hold a brightly coloured object approximately 20 cm from the baby's face and move it slowly side to side.
milestones.question: Does the baby swipe or bat their arms toward the moving object?

milestones.title: Coos and makes vowel sounds
milestones.description: Cooing is the earliest intentional vocalisation. It reflects intact hearing, auditory processing, and the beginning of the motor control needed for speech.
milestones.instruction: Talk softly to the baby and then pause. Observe their response in a quiet environment.
milestones.question: Does the baby make soft cooing or vowel sounds such as 'ooh' or 'aah'?

milestones.title: Turns head toward sounds
milestones.description: Orienting to sound is a critical indicator of hearing function and auditory localisation. Absence of this response warrants immediate hearing assessment.
milestones.instruction: Make a soft sound — a clap, bell, or voice — from one side of the baby without them seeing you. Do not touch them.
milestones.question: Does the baby turn their head toward the source of the sound?

milestones.title: Tracks moving object with eyes
milestones.description: Smooth visual tracking requires intact visual acuity, extraocular muscle coordination, and early cortical visual processing. This milestone also feeds directly into the Eye Tracking module's baseline assessment.
milestones.instruction: Hold a brightly coloured object 20 cm from the baby's eyes. Move it slowly from left to right across their visual field.
milestones.question: Does the baby follow the moving object smoothly with their eyes across the midline?

milestones.title: Shows interest in faces
milestones.description: Preferential attention to human faces is mediated by specialised face-processing neural circuits and is one of the earliest indicators of intact social cognition.
milestones.instruction: Position your face approximately 20–30 cm from the baby's face. Make a neutral expression first, then slowly smile.
milestones.question: Does the baby gaze at your face and show interest by focusing or stilling?

milestones.title: Social smile
milestones.description: A social smile — as distinct from a reflex smile during sleep — is the most significant milestone of this age group. It marks the onset of intentional social engagement and is a key early indicator assessed in autism screening tools.
milestones.instruction: Make eye contact with the baby and smile warmly at them. Speak softly.
milestones.question: Does the baby smile back at you in response to your smile or voice?

milestones.title: Makes eye contact
milestones.description: Sustained voluntary eye contact by 3 months is a foundational social-cognitive behaviour. Absence or avoidance of eye contact is a monitored early marker in developmental surveillance.
milestones.instruction: Position yourself face-to-face with the baby at their eye level. Observe whether they meet and hold your gaze.
milestones.question: Does the baby make and briefly hold eye contact with you?

milestones.title: Rolls from tummy to back
milestones.description: Rolling from prone to supine is the first full-body transitional movement and indicates sufficient trunk rotation and asymmetric limb coordination.
milestones.instruction: Place the baby on their tummy on a safe, flat surface. Observe for up to two minutes. Do not prompt them.
milestones.question: Does the baby roll from their tummy onto their back on their own?

milestones.title: Sits with support
milestones.description: Supported sitting demonstrates sufficient axial tone and head-righting reactions to maintain an upright position against gravity when the trunk is externally supported.
milestones.instruction: Seat the baby upright and support their trunk with both hands. Gradually reduce your support to test how much they hold themselves.
milestones.question: Does the baby hold their head steady and bear some of their own weight while seated with trunk support?

milestones.title: Bears weight on legs when held standing
milestones.description: Lower limb weight-bearing when supported standing reflects developing extensor muscle tone and is a precursor to independent standing development.
milestones.instruction: Hold the baby upright with their feet touching a firm surface. Provide trunk support but allow legs to be free.
milestones.question: Does the baby push down and bear some weight through their legs?

milestones.title: Reaches and grasps objects
milestones.description: Voluntary reaching with grasp integrates visual localisation with coordinated arm extension and palmar grip. Absence of reaching by 5 months is a developmental concern.
milestones.instruction: Hold a small, brightly coloured toy within the baby's reach. Wait for them to initiate reaching without guiding their hand.
milestones.question: Does the baby reach out and grasp the toy?

milestones.title: Transfers object from hand to hand
milestones.description: Hand-to-hand transfer requires bimanual coordination, midline crossing, and bilateral integration — skills that prefigure later tool use and writing.
milestones.instruction: Place a small toy in one of the baby's hands. Observe for up to one minute.
milestones.question: Does the baby transfer the toy from one hand to the other?

milestones.title: Babbles with consonant sounds
milestones.description: Canonical babbling with consonant-vowel combinations such as 'ba', 'ma', 'da' marks a critical transition in speech-motor development and auditory-vocal feedback loop maturation.
milestones.instruction: Observe the baby during a wakeful, alert period. Engage them in face-to-face interaction and then pause to listen.
milestones.question: Does the baby produce babbling sounds that include consonants such as 'ba', 'ma', or 'da'?

milestones.title: Responds to own name
milestones.description: Name recognition by 6 months reflects early word-form learning, auditory discrimination, and social attention — all prerequisites for language acquisition.
milestones.instruction: Call the baby's name clearly from behind or to the side. Do not gesture or touch. Wait five seconds.
milestones.question: Does the baby turn toward you or respond when you call their name?

milestones.title: Explores objects by mouthing and banging
milestones.description: Oral and tactile exploration of objects is the primary means of object knowledge acquisition at this stage and reflects developing sensorimotor schemas.
milestones.instruction: Give the baby a safe, age-appropriate toy. Observe their interaction for one to two minutes.
milestones.question: Does the baby mouth, shake, or bang the object to explore it — rather than simply holding it passively?

milestones.title: Finds partially hidden objects
milestones.description: Searching for a partially visible object is an early form of object permanence — the understanding that objects continue to exist when partially out of sight.
milestones.instruction: Let the baby watch as you cover a toy with a cloth, leaving part of the toy visible. Do not gesture toward the toy.
milestones.question: Does the baby reach for or look at the toy that is partially hidden under the cloth?

milestones.title: Smiles spontaneously at familiar people
milestones.description: Spontaneous social smiling — without prompting — at familiar caregivers indicates consolidated social recognition and attachment formation.
milestones.instruction: Approach the baby naturally without exaggerated facial expression. Observe their spontaneous reaction.
milestones.question: Does the baby smile at you spontaneously when they see you, without you smiling first?

milestones.title: Shows distress when caregiver leaves
milestones.description: Separation anxiety emerging at this stage reflects consolidating attachment and the early development of object permanence applied to people.
milestones.instruction: While the baby is calm and settled, the primary caregiver should leave the room without making a fuss. Observe the baby's response.
milestones.question: Does the baby show distress — crying, reaching, or fussing — when the caregiver leaves?

milestones.title: Sits without support
milestones.description: Independent sitting requires active trunk stabilisation through co-contraction of spinal extensors and flexors. It is a WHO gross motor milestone with a defined expected age window.
milestones.instruction: Place the baby in a seated position on a firm surface and remove your support completely. Stay close for safety.
milestones.question: Does the baby sit upright without any support for at least five seconds?

milestones.title: Crawls or commando crawls
milestones.description: Crawling, whether on all fours or in a commando style on the abdomen, represents a critical locomotor milestone. Either pattern is developmentally acceptable at this stage.
milestones.instruction: Place the baby on their tummy and place a toy just out of reach. Observe for any attempt to move toward it.
milestones.question: Does the baby crawl or commando-crawl toward objects they want?

milestones.title: Pulls to stand using furniture
milestones.description: Pulling to a standing position against furniture demonstrates sufficient upper and lower limb strength, balance reactions, and goal-directed motor planning.
milestones.instruction: Place the baby near a sturdy low table or sofa. Place a toy on the surface above them. Observe their attempt to stand.
milestones.question: Does the baby pull themselves up to a standing position by holding onto furniture?

milestones.title: Pincer grasp emerging
milestones.description: The emerging pincer grasp — using thumb and index finger — marks the transition from palmar raking to precise digital manipulation, a critical fine motor milestone.
milestones.instruction: Place a small puffed snack or small soft object on a flat surface within the baby's reach.
milestones.question: Does the baby attempt to pick up the small object using their thumb and index finger rather than their whole hand?

milestones.title: Bangs objects together
milestones.description: Purposeful bilateral hand use to bang objects together demonstrates bimanual coordination and intentional tool-like object interaction.
milestones.instruction: Give the baby two small blocks or toys, one in each hand. Observe what they do.
milestones.question: Does the baby bang the two objects together intentionally?

milestones.title: Babbles in long strings
milestones.description: Reduplicated and variegated babbling in extended strings — 'babababa', 'mamama' — reflects advancing phonological development and is predictive of vocabulary size at 18 months.
milestones.instruction: Engage the baby in playful interaction and then observe their spontaneous vocalisations.
milestones.question: Does the baby produce long strings of babbling sounds with varied consonants and vowels?

milestones.title: Understands 'no'
milestones.description: Comprehension of the word 'no' as a prohibition signal is among the earliest receptive vocabulary milestones and reflects early word-meaning mapping.
milestones.instruction: When the baby reaches for something they should not touch, say 'no' in a firm, calm voice without gesturing.
milestones.question: Does the baby pause or stop their action when you say 'no'?

milestones.title: Full object permanence
milestones.description: Searching for a completely hidden object demonstrates the consolidation of object permanence — the understanding that objects exist independent of perception, a key Piagetian milestone.
milestones.instruction: Let the baby watch as you hide a toy completely under a cloth. Do not leave any part visible.
milestones.question: Does the baby lift the cloth to retrieve the hidden toy?

milestones.title: Shows stranger anxiety
milestones.description: Wariness of unfamiliar adults reflects the formation of selective attachment to primary caregivers and is a normative and expected social-emotional development.
milestones.instruction: Have an unfamiliar adult approach the baby calmly and make eye contact. Observe the baby's reaction.
milestones.question: Does the baby show wariness, clinging, or distress in the presence of unfamiliar people?

milestones.title: Waves bye-bye when prompted
milestones.description: Imitative waving in response to a social cue demonstrates gestural imitation and early understanding of communicative intent.
milestones.instruction: Wave at the baby and say 'bye-bye' in a warm, animated voice. Do this two to three times.
milestones.question: Does the baby wave back or attempt to imitate the waving gesture?

milestones.title: Stands independently
milestones.description: Independent unsupported standing requires mature balance responses, sufficient lower limb strength, and postural control. Average age of attainment is 11 months per WHO Motor Development Study.
milestones.instruction: Support the baby to a standing position near a surface. Then slowly withdraw your support and observe.
milestones.question: Does the baby stand on their own without holding onto anything for at least two seconds?

milestones.title: Walks with one hand held
milestones.description: Walking with single-hand support is a transition milestone between cruising and independent walking, reflecting improving balance and gait patterning.
milestones.instruction: Hold one of the baby's hands and walk with them across the room.
milestones.question: Does the baby walk alongside you with only one hand held for support?

milestones.title: Mature pincer grasp
milestones.description: A mature pincer grasp — precise opposition of thumb tip and index finger tip — marks the completion of digital grasp development and enables manipulation of very small objects.
milestones.instruction: Place a small object such as a puffed snack or cereal piece on a flat surface.
milestones.question: Does the baby pick up the small object using the tips of their thumb and index finger precisely?

milestones.title: Puts objects into a container
milestones.description: Placing objects into a container demonstrates voluntary object release — the developmental complement to voluntary grasp — and early spatial understanding.
milestones.instruction: Give the baby a small block and place an open container in front of them. Demonstrate dropping an object in once.
milestones.question: Does the baby place or drop the block into the container?

milestones.title: Says first meaningful word
milestones.description: Production of a first true word — consistently using a sound sequence to refer to a specific person, object, or action — marks the onset of expressive language.
milestones.instruction: Ask the caregiver whether the baby uses any consistent sound or word with the same meaning across different situations.
milestones.question: Does the baby consistently use at least one word or sound to refer to a specific person, object, or action?

milestones.title: Uses gestures to communicate
milestones.description: Intentional communicative gestures — pointing, reaching, giving — are among the strongest early predictors of later language development and are key pre-linguistic milestones.
milestones.instruction: Place an interesting toy or object out of reach. Observe the baby's behaviour.
milestones.question: Does the baby use pointing, reaching, or giving to communicate a want or to direct your attention?

milestones.title: Imitates actions and gestures
milestones.description: Deferred and immediate imitation of observed actions reflects mirror neuron system maturation and is foundational to social learning and tool use.
milestones.instruction: Perform a simple action with a toy — such as banging it or pushing it — and encourage the baby to do the same.
milestones.question: Does the baby imitate the action you just demonstrated?

milestones.title: Joint attention — follows pointing gesture
milestones.description: Following a pointing gesture to look at a shared referent is the hallmark of joint attention — the ability to share focus on an external object with another person. Its absence by 12 months is a primary early marker in autism screening.
milestones.instruction: Point to an object across the room and say its name. Do not look at the baby while pointing — look at the object.
milestones.question: Does the baby follow your pointing finger and look at the object you are pointing to?

milestones.title: Walks independently
milestones.description: Independent walking is the primary locomotor milestone of early toddlerhood. The WHO median age is 12 months; failure to walk independently by 18 months warrants referral.
milestones.instruction: Observe the child walking across an open space without prompting or support.
milestones.question: Does the child walk independently across the room without holding onto anything?

milestones.title: Vocabulary of at least three words
milestones.description: A minimum vocabulary of three to five true words by 15 months is a key language milestone. Fewer than three words by 18 months is a red flag requiring speech and language evaluation.
milestones.instruction: Ask the caregiver to list the words the child uses consistently and meaningfully.
milestones.question: Does the child use at least three different words consistently and meaningfully?

milestones.title: Initiates joint attention by pointing
milestones.description: Protodeclarative pointing — pointing to share interest in something, not just to request it — is a higher-order joint attention skill and a critical early marker in developmental surveillance for autism spectrum conditions.
milestones.instruction: Observe the child's spontaneous behaviour. Note whether they point to show you things they find interesting, not just to ask for them.
milestones.question: Does the child point to show you something interesting — not just to ask for something they want?

milestones.title: Combines two words
milestones.description: Two-word combinations — 'more milk', 'daddy go', 'big dog' — mark the onset of syntactic development. Absence of two-word combinations by 24 months is a primary language delay red flag.
milestones.instruction: Ask the caregiver whether the child ever puts two words together to say something.
milestones.question: Does the child combine two different words together, such as 'more juice' or 'mama go'?

milestones.title: Symbolic play
milestones.description: Using one object to represent another — a block as a phone, a spoon as an aeroplane — marks the onset of symbolic function, which underlies both language and early literacy.
milestones.instruction: Give the child a spoon and a doll or stuffed animal. Observe spontaneous play for two to three minutes.
milestones.question: Does the child use an object to represent something else — for example, pretending to feed a doll with a spoon?

milestones.title: Runs without falling
milestones.description: Running with good balance and direction changes reflects mature reciprocal gait and postural reactions. Frequent unexplained falling warrants neurological or musculoskeletal assessment.
milestones.instruction: Observe the child running freely in an open space.
milestones.question: Does the child run without falling in a coordinated way?

milestones.title: Uses two to three word sentences
milestones.description: Multi-word utterances beyond two-word combinations signal advancing syntactic development. By 30 months most children produce three-word sentences reliably.
milestones.instruction: Observe the child's spontaneous speech during play or conversation.
milestones.question: Does the child use sentences of two to three words regularly during play or conversation?

milestones.title: Sorts objects by shape or colour
milestones.description: Categorisation by perceptual attribute — shape, colour, size — reflects early conceptual development and the ability to apply abstract rules across object sets.
milestones.instruction: Place a set of blocks of two different colours in front of the child. Ask them to put the same-colour ones together.
milestones.question: Does the child sort the blocks by colour or shape correctly?

milestones.title: Hops on one foot
milestones.description: Single-leg hopping requires dynamic balance, unilateral lower limb strength, and motor planning. It is a reliable marker of neuromotor maturation at this age.
milestones.instruction: Demonstrate hopping on one foot and ask the child to do the same. Allow two or three attempts.
milestones.question: Does the child hop on one foot at least twice without falling?

milestones.title: Speaks in full sentences
milestones.description: By 3 to 4 years, typical development includes consistent use of grammatically structured sentences with subject, verb, and object. Speech should be understood by strangers at least 75% of the time.
milestones.instruction: Engage the child in a short conversation about something familiar such as their family or a recent activity.
milestones.question: Does the child speak in complete sentences that strangers can mostly understand?

milestones.title: Draws a circle when shown
milestones.description: Copying a circle requires integration of visual discrimination, motor planning, and graphic motor execution. It is the earliest reliably assessed drawing milestone.
milestones.instruction: Draw a circle in front of the child and then give them a pencil or crayon and ask them to draw one.
milestones.question: Does the child draw a recognisable closed circle after being shown?

milestones.title: Skips alternating feet
milestones.description: Skipping requires the integration of hopping and stepping in an alternating pattern, demanding bilateral coordination, timing, and rhythm — advanced neuromotor skills.
milestones.instruction: Demonstrate skipping and ask the child to skip across the room.
milestones.question: Does the child skip with an alternating foot pattern rather than a gallop?

milestones.title: Cuts paper with scissors
milestones.description: Using scissors requires a mature tripod pencil grip adapted to a bimanual tool, bilateral hand coordination, and planning of continuous cutting movements.
milestones.instruction: Give the child a pair of child-safe scissors and a strip of paper. Ask them to cut it.
milestones.question: Does the child hold and use scissors to cut across a strip of paper?

milestones.title: Tells a simple story or describes an event
milestones.description: Narrative ability — sequencing events into a coherent story with characters, actions, and outcomes — is the highest-level language milestone in this age range and a strong predictor of later literacy.
milestones.instruction: Ask the child to tell you about something they did today or to tell you a story about a picture.
milestones.question: Does the child produce a sequence of related ideas or events in a way that makes sense?

milestones.title: Counts five or more objects correctly
milestones.description: One-to-one correspondence in counting — touching each object once while saying a number word — requires coordination of verbal sequence memory with motor action and is the foundation of arithmetic.
milestones.instruction: Place five objects in a row in front of the child and ask them to count them.
milestones.question: Does the child count five objects correctly by touching each one once?

milestones.title: Cooperative play with peers
milestones.description: True cooperative play — where children work toward a shared goal, negotiate roles, and take turns — represents the highest developmental level of play and reflects mature theory of mind and social cognition.
milestones.instruction: Observe the child playing with at least one other child of similar age for five minutes.
milestones.question: Does the child engage in cooperative play — sharing, taking turns, and working toward a common goal with other children?
